nameStory: Despite its name, marshelder isn't actually an elder at all! The 'marsh' part comes from its love of wet, muddy places, while 'elder' refers to its somewhat similar-looking leaves that reminded early settlers of elderberry plants. It's also called giant sumpweed, which hints at its impressive size and weedy nature.
description: Marshelder is a towering annual plant that can grow anywhere from 1.5 to 6 feet tall, making it hard to miss once it gets established. This sturdy member of the sunflower family has thick, upright stems and large, coarse leaves that give it a robust, weedy appearance. Unlike many of its showier sunflower relatives, marshelder produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers that you might overlook at first glance. It's a prairie native that has wandered far from home and now pops up across much of North America.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy annual with thick, erect stems that feel ridged or grooved when you run your fingers along them. The stems are grayish-green and usually unbranched, giving the whole plant a bold, upright appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, coarse leaves with rough, sandpapery texture that are arranged alternately along the stem. The leaves have a somewhat triangular or heart-shaped outline with toothed edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish, unremarkable flower heads clustered at the top of the plant. Unlike typical sunflower family members, these flowers lack showy petals and look more like tiny green buttons.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are hairless near the base but develop fine, curved or curled hairs toward the top. The surface feels finely ridged and has a distinctive grayish-green color.

habitat: In New England, marshelder is quite rare but occasionally turns up in disturbed soils, waste areas, and edges of agricultural fields. It prefers rich, moist soils and can sometimes be found near wetlands or in areas with seasonal flooding. Look for it in places where the soil has been recently disturbed or where other weedy species thrive.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as the soil warms, starting as small rosettes with their characteristic rough-textured leaves becoming apparent.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach their full impressive height and produce their small, inconspicuous greenish flower clusters at the stem tops during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers develop into small, hard fruits and the entire plant begins to turn brown and dry out as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through winter as dried stalks, but the annual plant has completed its life cycle.

funFact: Marshelder seeds are sometimes accidentally included in wild bird seed mixes, which is actually how this prairie wanderer has spread to places like Britain and Ireland - it literally hitchhiked across the ocean in birdfeeders!
confusionNotes: The large, coarse leaves might remind you of giant ragweed, but marshelder's stems are much more ridged and grayish-green, plus it typically grows more upright and unbranched. Remember: marshelder has ridged stems, ragweed has round, hairy stems.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this plant is neither a true elder (Sambucus) nor necessarily found in marshes. The common name reflects early settlers' tendency to name new plants after familiar ones from home, even when they weren't closely related.
compareHints: Marshelder is the only species in its genus Cyclachaena in our region, making it unique among local sunflower family members. Compared to other large, weedy members of the sunflower family like giant ragweed, marshelder stands out with its distinctive ridged, grayish stems and more compact, unbranched growth habit. Its small, petal-less flowers also set it apart from most of its showier sunflower relatives.
